fuller.text: This encyclopedia article explains race: a way of sorting people into groups by shared physical or social traits, groups a society treats as distinct. Its central claim is that modern science sees race as a social construct, an identity assigned by rules a society makes. Race is partly based on physical likeness, but the article says it has no built-in biological meaning. Different cultures draw the groups differently, and the lines change over time.

fuller.text: The article says the idea of race is the foundation of racism, the belief that some races are superior to others. Even scholars who call race a construct mostly agree it has real effects on people's lives, through favoritism and discrimination built into institutions. Groups with little power are often shut out or oppressed, and racism has led to slavery and genocide.

fuller.text: The modern idea of race grew out of European colonial projects from the 16th to 18th centuries, which defined race by skin color and body differences. Early scientific schemes mixed description with prejudice, always placing white Europeans at the top. In 1735, Carl Linnaeus split humans into four continental varieties, calling Europeans active and adventurous and Africans lazy and careless. Johann Blumenbach's five-group scheme of 1775 already noted that one group shades into the next, with no clear limits between them.

fuller.text: The main case against biological races comes from how human genetic differences are spread out. Most variation is within groups: on average about 85% lies within local populations, about 7% between nearby populations, and about 8% between continents. One African population holds about 100% of human genetic diversity, while the least diverse population studied holds only about 60%. Traits change gradually across the map in clines, meaning smooth gradients, rather than stopping at sharp borders. In biology, race usually means subspecies, a distinct population within a species, but human groups are neither cut off by geography nor different enough to qualify.

fuller.text: Some researchers push back on this picture. A. W. F. Edwards argued in 2003 that combining many genetic markers, points in DNA where people differ, can sort people into clusters resembling traditional continental groups. Critics reply that the clusters depend on which populations a researcher chooses to sample. Sampling only Icelanders, Mayans and Maoris, for instance, would give three neat clusters, with everyone else looking like a mix of them. A 2007 study found that even with hundreds of markers, individuals are often more similar to members of other populations than to their own.

fuller.text: The article also tracks how experts' views have shifted, using surveys of scientists. In a 1985 survey, 41% of physical anthropologists disagreed that there are biological races in humans. When the survey was repeated in 1999, that share had risen to 69%. A 2017 survey of 3,286 American anthropologists found agreement that biological races do not exist, but that the social experience of race can affect health.

fuller.text: The piece shows the debate is not fully closed in every field. Forensic anthropologist George Gill argues that many skeletal features follow geography, and that denying races is often politically motivated. Norman Sauer answered that identifying race from a skeleton predicts the social label a person carried in life, not that races exist in nature. In 2023, a US National Academies report said researchers should not use race as a stand-in for human genetic variation.

fuller.text: Scholars still debate how far racial categories rest on biology versus social choice. Geneticist David Reich argues that ancestry differences matching today's racial groups are real; 67 scientists replied that the groups' meaning comes from society. The article's overall conclusion matches a 2019 statement by physical anthropologists: humans are not biologically divided into distinct racial types, and the Western race concept arose from colonialism.

brief.text: This encyclopedia article is about race: sorting people into groups by shared looks or social traits. It matters because the idea of race is the base of racism. Racism has led to slavery and genocide, the killing of whole groups of people.

brief.text: Scientists now see race as a social construct: groups defined by society's rules, not by biology. On average, about 85% of human genetic difference is found within local groups, not between them. Still, most scholars agree race has real effects, because people are treated better or worse by it.
